newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - Allianz and AIG - the titans.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - Allianz and AIG - the titans.

text.p: Big is best, but bigger is better. Two of the giants of the international insurance world - Germany's Allianz and the U.S.-based AIG, have reported profits ahead of industry trends and show every sign of increasing their ability to earn premium. Allianz has just taken over the renewal of $90m worth of high excess and energy business from the Fireman's fund insurance company, enhancing its position as a U.S. and global property casualty insurer.

In Australia, it is using its associate company MMI, which this week posted a 20 percent rise in half year 1996 profits to push further into Asia. MMI is in the process of acquiring 20 percent of Allianz Insurance (Singapore) by the end of March, and yesterday MMI managing director Pieter Franzen told Australian journalists he "expects to be making an announcement in a few weeks on an arrangement with local partners and Allianz in Asia to set up general insurance businesses".

Deregulation in its home market and the introduction of developments such as telephone-based insurance have led to an upbeat assessment of prospects in Germany. Meanwhile, Allianz has arrived in Poland, prompting the deputy director of insurance at the former state-run insurer PZU to predict he will lose market share to the German giant over the next three years. Allianz is also awaiting a licence in China, and has established a foothold in the Russian market, where although no major investments have been committed, there are high expectations of future premium.

Allianz shares the latter position with AIG, except that the U.S. insurer already has a licence to operate in China, indeed it was the first foreign insurer to get one. AIG yesterday reported that its 1996 pre-tax incomes topped $4 billion for the first time ever. A look through the accounts shows significant advances on almost every front, a record underwriting profit of $399 million, and a combined ratio down to 96.87.

Hank Greenberg attributed some of the company's continued success to an expanding middle class and growing privatisations in many of its most important overseas markets, but a massive number of new ventures in 1996 looks set to increase earnings potentials in the future. Aside from China and Russia, the end of the trade dispute with Japan (in which AIG played a large role) will be advantageous.

As with Allianz, AIG continues to make lucrative advances in the life sector, and is also growing in the field of speciality insurance products. So far there has never been a significant clash between these two titans. But with such momentum behind their expansion, can this last forever?
